model_finding_codes: Carburetor icing - conducive weather conditions|Use of carburetor heat - not performed - pilot|Fuel system - water contamination|Preflight inspection - not performed/inadequate - pilot|Personnel issues - engine power loss response
model_probable_cause: A total loss of engine power in the traffic pattern for reasons that could not be conclusively determined by postaccident examination (no mechanical anomalies were found), most consistent with carburetor icing given ambient temperature/dewpoint conditions that were on the border of serious icing at glide and cruise power, combined with the pilot's stated infrequent use of carburetor heat (which was found in the OFF position). A contributing factor was water contamination found in the fuel system, which the pilot knew about but did not re-check (sump) before the accident flight, and the pilot's delegation of the preflight inspection to the passenger. The subsequent loss of engine power at low altitude in the traffic pattern resulted in an off-airport forced landing/collision with terrain and a roadway.

ntsb_probable_cause: An in-flight collision with a bird while on approach.

model_top3: Gear-up landing / landing gear not extended|Landing gear collapse|Loss of control on approach
model_finding_codes: Aircraft-Landing gear extension/retraction system-Not used/mismanaged|Pilot-Use of checklist-Not followed|Personnel issue-Pilot-Task management/vigilance
model_probable_cause: Given the retractable-gear Cessna 177RG, benign VMC weather, approach phase of flight, and a no-injury outcome, the most consistent scenario is the pilot's failure to extend/verify the landing gear prior to landing (or a related gear malfunction), resulting in an abnormal landing gear event. Weather and pilot experience (360 total/229 in type) do not suggest weather or basic proficiency were primary factors; the pattern is typical of gear mismanagement events in retractable-gear singles rather than a weather- or mechanical-failure-driven accident.

ntsb_probable_cause: The non-instrument rated pilot’s improper decision to attempt flight into instrument meteorological conditions, which resulted in spatial disorientation and loss of control and subsequent impact with terrain.
model_top3: Loss of control in flight|Controlled flight into terrain|In-flight structural failure
model_finding_codes: Personnel issues-Pilot-Instrument flying skill-Poor|Environmental issues-Instrument meteorological conditions|Personnel issues-Decision making-Poor (self-induced pressure to continue flight)|Aircraft-Spatial disorientation|Personnel issues-Pilot-Lack of instrument rating|Aircraft-Flight control system-Overstress separation (result of loss of control)
model_probable_cause: The pilot's decision to depart at night into deteriorating weather conditions without an instrument rating and with inadequate instrument proficiency, which resulted in spatial disorientation and subsequent loss of airplane control while in instrument meteorological conditions. This led to an in-flight overstress/breakup (or high-speed impact) with the terrain/water. Contributing factors were the pilot's self-imposed pressure to reach the destination, his known poor instrument flying skills as assessed by his flight instructor, and the forecast/observed IMC (fog, low ceilings) along the route at night over featureless terrain (water/wilderness), which would have provided no visual horizon reference.

ntsb_probable_cause: A fatigue fracture of the nose landing gear scissor link, which resulted in a separation of the nose landing gear piston assembly.
model_top3: Landing gear collapse (nose)|Nose over/Overturn|Loss of control on landing
model_finding_codes: Nose landing gear scissor link - fatigue failure|Landing gear component - inadequate inspection|Maintenance - improper inspection (landing gear linkage not inspected per AD 43 Appendix D)
model_probable_cause: The fatigue failure of the nose landing gear upper scissor link during touchdown, which resulted in separation of the nose landing gear strut/cylinder and led to the airplane nosing over. Contributing to the accident was the lack of a manufacturer-specified inspection requirement for the scissor link, despite regulatory (14 CFR Part 43, Appendix D) requirements to inspect landing gear linkages for fatigue and wear, which likely allowed the fatigue crack to go undetected during prior maintenance/inspections.

ntsb_probable_cause: The failure of the spring pin in the right propeller governor, which precluded the pilot from controlling the propeller pitch to maintain engine rpm, resulting in a loss of engine thrust, excessive drag, and the subsequent forced landing to a field.
model_occurrence: Loss of engine power (partial) - Propeller/governor malfunction
model_top3: Loss of engine power (partial)|Powerplant system/component failure|Forced landing/emergency landing
model_finding_codes: Aircraft-Powerplant-Propeller governor-Failure|Aircraft-Powerplant-Propeller pitch control-Malfunction|Personnel issues-Decision making-Pilot-Diversion/forced landing (not causal)|Miscellaneous-Investigation-Undetermined shear load source
model_probable_cause: The in-flight fracture (shear overload) of the right engine propeller governor's spring pin, which allowed the pilot spool to shift and directed high-pressure oil to drive the propeller toward low pitch, causing an uncommanded engine/propeller rpm runaway and subsequent loss of effective engine power. This necessitated a forced, gear-up landing in a field short of the diversion airport. The specific source of the shear loading on the spring pin could not be determined (no fatigue, binding, or foreign material contamination was found).
